v-l-arpege.name: L'Arpège
v-l-arpege.why: Passard put down the knife on red meat back in 2001 and picked up a trowel — a full generation before the plant world caught up with him. He is largely self-taught, having learned the grill under Alain Senderens at L'Archestrate, the very address he later took over and renamed.
v-l-arpege.verdict: One of the most influential kitchens in modern Paris, and you can trace the bloodline: alumni run Septime (Bertrand Grébaut trained here) and Le Servan (Tatiana Levha, ex-Arpège, ex-Astrance). In July 2025 Passard went further than anyone at his level, striking meat, fish, shellfish, dairy and eggs from the menu — the first three-star in the world to do it, with only honey from his own hives surviving. Come for the vegetables off his own gardens, not for value, and not for the egg you've read about.
v-l-arpege.signature: The house was built on the chaud-froid d'oeuf, the "Arpège egg": a warm farm-egg yolk under cold four-spice cream sharpened with sherry vinegar and chives, a thread of maple, served in its own shell. Verify before you count on it — the July 2025 plant-based turn stripped eggs, cream and butter, so what reaches the table now is the garden: vegetables, fruit, herbs and flowers from Passard's own plots in the Sarthe and by Mont-Saint-Michel.
v-l-arpege.caveat: Not a value eat. Dinner tasting menus run roughly 420 to 540 euros (a lunch menu is nearer 175), and since July 2025 the animal cooking that made his name — the lobster, the pigeon — is gone. With meat, fish, shellfish, dairy and eggs all struck, the kitchen is now all-vegetable but for the honey from its own hives, so read it as near-vegan rather than strictly so. Portions can feel small for the money, and a table is hard-won.

signal_chip.label: 3 MICHELIN Stars
signal_chip.full: Three MICHELIN Stars, Guide MICHELIN France 2026

v-plenitude-cheval-blanc-paris.name: Plénitude - Cheval Blanc Paris
v-plenitude-cheval-blanc-paris.why: Before Paris, Donckele spent two decades earning three stars at La Vague d'Or in Saint-Tropez — a Riviera career he walked away from to open in the LVMH-owned Samaritaine, the reborn Art Nouveau department store on the Seine.
v-plenitude-cheval-blanc-paris.address: Cheval Blanc Paris, 8 Quai du Louvre, 75001 Paris
v-plenitude-cheval-blanc-paris.verdict: Donckele's second three-star kitchen, and one that lived up to its billing rather than coasting on the Cheval Blanc name: three MICHELIN stars in barely seven months - awarded at the March 2022 Cognac ceremony, straight from zero to three - and held every year since, through the 2026 guide, backed by Gault&Millau 19/20 (five toques) and No. 14 on the World's 50 Best 2025. Here the sauce, not the protein, is the dish.
v-plenitude-cheval-blanc-paris.signature: The sauces themselves. Donckele works as a self-styled saucier-parfumeur, numbering his layered sauces like perfumes into what he calls his "Absolues," and the two carte-blanche menus (Fuguons ensemble in 4 acts, Symphonie in 6) are built so that langoustine, turbot or pigeon serve as condiments to their broths, vinaigrettes and jus - named plates like La Langoustine Sabayon Cardinal Thenors and Turbot Tellurienne d'Hiver, reported by Fine Dining Lovers. Pastry by Maxime Frédéric, named World's Best Pastry Chef 2025.
v-plenitude-cheval-blanc-paris.caveat: Not a discovery, a summit - and priced like one. The six-act Symphonie ran EUR 480 in 2025 (the four-act Fuguons ensemble EUR 445), with wine pairings up to EUR 495 on top; dinner only, Tuesday to Saturday, in a hushed 26-seat room above the Seine. The sauce-as-hero concept is cerebral and formal by design - go for the thrill of watching a master saucier work, not for comfort food or a casual night.

signal_chip.label: No. 14 - World's 50 Best 2025
signal_chip.full: Ranked No. 14 on The World's 50 Best Restaurants 2025 (up four places from 2024); its pastry chef Maxime Frédéric took the World's Best Pastry Chef award the same year.

v-kei.name: Kei
v-kei.why: A boy in Nagano, son of a kaiseki cook, watched a documentary about French cuisine on Japanese television and decided that would be his life. He moved to France in 1998 and cooked for years under Gilles Goujon and then Alain Ducasse before opening his own small room off the rue Coq-Héron in 2011.
v-kei.verdict: France's only Japanese-born three-star chef, and the room has held all three MICHELIN stars every year since 2020 — this is precision plated as spectacle, not comfort or improvisation.
v-kei.signature: Le jardin de légumes croquants — a "garden" of up to forty seasonal ingredients, crisp raw vegetables and herbs layered over Scottish smoked salmon, bound with a rocket cream and tomato vinaigrette and crowned with a cloud of lemon foam and a black-olive-and-almond crumble. It took five years to perfect and shifts with the season, so no two plates are quite alike.
v-kei.caveat: This is ceremony and expense, not a spontaneous dinner. The cheapest way in is a €195 Discovery menu served only at Friday and Saturday lunch; the full tastings run €290 to €580 (the restaurant notes prices are subject to change). The room is small, and reservations — which open on the first Tuesday of each month, two months ahead — go fast. Go for the craft, not for warmth.
v-kei.person: Kei Kobayashi — chef-owner. Born in Nagano, Japan, the son of a traditional kaiseki cook; he turned to French cooking after watching a documentary about French cuisine, moved to France in 1998, and trained under Gilles Goujon (Auberge du Vieux Puits) and Alain Ducasse before opening Kei in 2011.

signal_chip.label: MICHELIN 3 stars
signal_chip.full: Three MICHELIN stars since 2020, retained in the 2026 Guide — Kei Kobayashi was the first Japanese chef to earn three stars in France.

v-table-by-bruno-verjus.name: Table by Bruno Verjus
v-table-by-bruno-verjus.why: Verjus came to the stove only in his mid-fifties, after lives as a medical student, an entrepreneur in China, a photographer and a radio food critic, opening Table by the Marché d'Aligre in 2013 — the market he still shops each morning before service.
v-table-by-bruno-verjus.verdict: The two MICHELIN stars and the No. 8-in-the-world ranking are earned, not hype: one daily seating at a wave-shaped counter, Verjus plating in front of you, ingredient-worship over technique for its own sake. Book it and you'll watch a self-taught ex-food-critic cook the day's tide and fields into a single 'Couleur du jour' tasting.
v-table-by-bruno-verjus.signature: Lobster 'mi-cru mi-cuit' — half-raw, half-cooked, trap-caught off the Ile d'Yeu, the shells toasted and the flesh warmed in ghee to roughly the temperature of the mouth — the dish critics reach for first when they describe him. The meal ends, as it always does, on his chocolate-and-caper tart under a spoon of caviar.
v-table-by-bruno-verjus.caveat: It slipped from No. 3 (2024) to No. 8 (2025) on The World's 50 Best — still elite, but the trajectory points down, not up. There's one set seating, no a la carte, only the fixed daily tasting (reported around EUR 480, subject to change) at a counter of roughly two dozen seats, with a non-refundable deposit taken at booking — so the real obstacle is landing a reservation, and you don't get to choose your dishes.
v-table-by-bruno-verjus.person: Bruno Verjus, chef-patron, in his mid-sixties. Self-taught cook with a scattered pedigree before the stove: former medical student, entrepreneur in China, photographer, author and radio food critic. He came to the kitchen only in his mid-fifties, opened Table in 2013, and took it to two MICHELIN stars and the World's 50 Best top ten.

signal_chip.label: No. 8 - World's 50 Best 2025
signal_chip.full: Ranked No. 8 on The World's 50 Best Restaurants 2025 (down from No. 3 in 2024, in the top 10 since its 2023 debut); two MICHELIN stars in the 2025 and 2026 MICHELIN Guide France.
signal_chip.cosign: The World's 50 Best Restaurants 2025 + MICHELIN Guide France 2026

v-table-by-bruno-verjus._lane: The new haute — the produce and the fire

v-datil.name: Datil
v-datil.why: Before Manon Fleury cooked for anyone she fenced sabre for France, and something of that discipline survives here in a hierarchy-free, women-led brigade where no one shouts across the line. It is the table that made 'sustainable' stop sounding like an apology.
v-datil.verdict: One of Paris's clearest proofs that a near-meatless tasting menu can carry a MICHELIN star — and, since 2026, a Green Star — without a single luxury crutch: no caviar, no wagyu, no truffle-for-show, animal protein used only as a condiment.
v-datil.signature: The zero-waste tasting menu: it opens with a bouillon drawn from vegetable peelings (potato peel, at last report) and closes with a tisane brewed from plum stones — a nod to the restaurant's name. Plants lead; meat plays a background extra.
v-datil.caveat: Tasting menu only, and not cheap — the restaurant's own site now lists EUR 95 for a five-course lunch and EUR 160 for a seven-course dinner (wine pairings EUR 65 / EUR 85); older Le Fooding listings still show EUR 65 / EUR 120, so prices have climbed — check when booking. A small room that books out fast, and if you want meat at the centre of the plate, this is the wrong table.
v-datil.person: Manon Fleury — chef-owner, a former French junior sabre-fencing champion who trained at Ferrandi and cooked at L'Astrance (under Pascal Barbot) and Blue Hill at Stone Barns (under Dan Barber), then ran the kitchens at Le Mermoz, Elsa at the Monte-Carlo Beach and Le Perchoir before opening Datil in September 2023. Co-chef Laurene Barjhoux (ex-Arpege / Alain Passard) runs the hierarchy-free, women-led brigade beside her.

signal_chip.label: 1★ + Green Star
signal_chip.full: 1 MICHELIN Star (2024) and MICHELIN Green Star (2026)

v-datil._lane: The new haute — the produce and the fire

v-le-rigmarole.name: Le Rigmarole
tags: Binchotan yakitori x handmade Italian pasta
productTags: Binchotan yakitori x handmade Italian pasta
v-le-rigmarole.why: They met over the pass at Guy Savoy, an American-Taiwanese pastry commis and a Franco-American cook, cooked their way through three-star kitchens in Paris and New York, and then opened a walnut counter of their own — where his Japanese charcoal and her Italian pasta finally eat off the same menu.
v-le-rigmarole.subcat: Binchotan yakitori x handmade Italian pasta
v-le-rigmarole.verdict: One MICHELIN star, held since 2020 and still standing in the 2026 guide, for a walnut counter where Robert Compagnon grills yakitori over Japanese binchotan while the kitchen rolls its pasta by hand. The spaghetti with bottarga is the plate regulars come back for; the tasting-menu seats are few and go early, so plan ahead.
v-le-rigmarole.signature: Spaghetti with bottarga: house-made pasta under a snow of grated cured mullet roe. Its charcoal-side twin is the yakitori "thigh," perfumed with clementine zest.
v-le-rigmarole.caveat: Small and counter-centric — a walnut bar plus a handful of tables, not a big room. It is tasting-menu-driven, books up, and is not cheap, so treat it as a plan-ahead splurge rather than a walk-in. Hours and format have shifted over time (mid-week tastings, more casual weekend and lunch service), so check what is on before you go.

signal_chip.label: 1 MICHELIN Star
signal_chip.full: One MICHELIN Star, awarded 2020 and retained in the 2026 guide; also carried on the World's 50 Best Discovery list.

v-le-rigmarole._lane: The new haute — the produce and the fire

v-le-grand-vefour.name: Le Grand Véfour
v-le-grand-vefour.why: Napoléon is said to have courted Joséphine at these tables; Victor Hugo kept to a fixed order of vermicelli and lamb; Colette, who lived upstairs in the Palais-Royal, was carried down on a chair to dine in her last years. It has traded here as the Café de Chartres since 1784.
v-le-grand-vefour.verdict: In 2026 this is not a starred restaurant and doesn't pretend to be — it's a listed 18th-century room under the Palais-Royal arcades where the banquettes still carry brass plaques for Napoléon, Victor Hugo and Colette, now serving Bruno Doucet's pleasure-first French menu with a new 150-seat garden terrace. Go for the room and the ghosts; as of this writing the cooking is unrated by MICHELIN or Gault&Millau, though early curated reviews run warm.
v-le-grand-vefour.signature: Gigot d'agneau de lait carved tableside and a soufflé glacé au Grand Marnier — anchors of Bruno Doucet's pleasure-first, tableside-service menu (Elite Traveler; Les Nouvelles Gastronomiques, 2026). The old-era emblem, Guy Martin's ravioles de foie gras "Prince Vladimir," retired with him at the end of 2025.
v-le-grand-vefour.caveat: Starless since MICHELIN pulled its last two stars in the 2021 guide, as Guy Martin steered the room toward simpler, lower-priced cooking (a full bistro by 2024); the May 2026 Paris Society relaunch under Doucet carries no star, and the menu is only weeks old and unproven by any authority. Sources vary on the exact reopening (Sortiraparis and Do It In Paris: 12 May 2026; Elite Traveler: "late May"). Come for the history and the listed neoclassical room — long called the prettiest in Paris — not for a ranking.
v-le-grand-vefour.person: Bruno Doucet (chef; owns La Régalade Saint-Honoré and Le Comptoir du Relais; trained under Barrier, Vigato and Gagnaire) — owner Paris Society / Laurent de Gourcuff (Accor)

signal_chip.label: Ex-MICHELIN 3★
signal_chip.full: Held three MICHELIN stars (2000–2008) and two until the 2021 guide, when the stars were withdrawn during Guy Martin's shift to accessible cooking; the 2026 Paris Society relaunch has no star. Historic pedigree, not a current ranking.

v-guy-savoy.name: Guy Savoy
v-guy-savoy.why: Six salons hung with contemporary art on loan from François Pinault's collection, floor-to-ceiling windows over the Seine, and a private lift up into the old royal mint — Savoy negotiated the whole piano nobile of the Monnaie de Paris as his dining room in 2015.
v-guy-savoy.address: 11 quai de Conti, 75006 Paris, France (Monnaie de Paris / Hotel de la Monnaie)
v-guy-savoy.verdict: Two MICHELIN stars in the 2026 Guide France (down from three since 2023), yet ranked joint World No. 1 by La Liste 2026 — a grand classical restaurant inside the Monnaie de Paris, the old royal mint, where the tasting menu (around EUR 490) still opens with the artichoke-and-black-truffle soup that has anchored his cooking for decades.
v-guy-savoy.signature: Soupe d'artichaut a la truffe noire — artichoke and black-truffle soup, served with a toasted mushroom-and-truffle brioche slicked in black-truffle butter; his longest-standing signature and the plate most often named as his defining dish.
v-guy-savoy.caveat: The "3 stars" billing is out of date: MICHELIN cut it to two in 2023 (it had held three since 2002) and has not restored the third. Its "world's best" standing comes from La Liste's algorithmic aggregator — and in 2026 that top spot is shared with nine other restaurants, all scoring 99.5/100 — not a single live-judged verdict. Dinner is a special-occasion outlay (roughly EUR 490 before wine); open only Wednesday to Saturday, with Saturday dinner-only.
v-guy-savoy.person: Guy Savoy (b. 24 July 1953, Nevers) — chef-owner. Apprenticed three years under Pierre and Jean Troisgros at Maison Troisgros in Roanne, then cooked at Lasserre before opening his own Paris table on rue Duret in 1980; moved into the Monnaie de Paris in 2015. His kitchen trained Gordon Ramsay and Richard Ekkebus among others.

signal_chip.label: La Liste 2026: joint World No. 1
signal_chip.full: Ranked joint No. 1 restaurant in the world by La Liste 2026 (99.5/100, tied with nine other tables across eight countries) — the ninth consecutive year Guy Savoy Paris has topped the aggregate ranking. Note: MICHELIN holds it at two stars in the 2026 Guide France, down from three since 2023.

v-le-train-bleu.name: Le Train Bleu
v-le-train-bleu.address: Place Louis Armand, 75012 Paris (1st floor, Gare de Lyon, Hall 1)
v-le-train-bleu.verdict: You come for the room, not the plate. The gilded 1901 dining room above Gare de Lyon — 41 painted panels and crystal chandeliers — was classified a monument historique in 1972, and it is the real event. The food, Michel Rostang's traditional brasserie repertoire since October 2018, is competent and deliberately safe: Gault&Millau rates it 12/20, "Table Gourmande," not a destination kitchen.
v-le-train-bleu.signature: Gigot d'agneau rôti — leg of lamb carved tableside from the trolley, with gratin dauphinois: the Train Bleu's tableside signature, kept on the card by Rostang. Crêpes Suzette, flambéed tableside, to finish.
v-le-train-bleu.caveat: Come for the Belle Époque room, not the cooking. Paris Unlocked found it "a bit safe" and "not always particularly inventive," with the pike-quenelle's Newburg sauce "curiously lacking in creaminess." Prices track the setting, not the kitchen.
v-le-train-bleu.person: Michel Rostang — whose eponymous Maison Rostang holds two Michelin stars (2025), though he handed its kitchen to Nicolas Beaumann in 2020 — has curated the menu since October 2018; Samir Balia has run the kitchen as head chef since 2019.

signal_chip.label: G&M 12/20 (2025)
signal_chip.full: Gault&Millau: 12/20, "Table Gourmande" — "Institution nationale, Le Train Bleu est autant une bonne brasserie qu'un monument," where Rostang "sans prendre trop de risque, assure sa partition" (fr.gaultmillau.com, 2025).

v-septime.name: Septime
v-septime.why: In 2011 a graphic-designer-turned-cook who had trained under Alain Passard at Arpege opened a plain oak-and-steel room on rue de Charonne with his high-school friend Theophile Pourriat. They meant to build a good bistro; instead they wrote the template half of Paris has been copying ever since.
v-septime.verdict: One MICHELIN star (held into the 2026 Guide) and No. 40 on The World's 50 Best 2025, yet lunch is five courses for 85 euros and there is no menu to choose from: you eat the carte blanche the kitchen sends, rewritten by the week's harvest. The neo-bistro that set the template for a generation of Paris kitchens, and still one of the hardest of them to book.
v-septime.signature: No fixed signature dish, by design: the carte blanche tasting menu is the whole offer, five steps at lunch, seven at dinner, driven by a near-obsessive micro-seasonality. Recent plates cited by The World's 50 Best: cepes and girolles in peppercorn sauce, and young leeks in a mussel-and-pimenton butter under wafer-thin lardo.
v-septime.caveat: Getting in is the trial, not the meal. Booking is online only, opens daily at 10am for three weeks out, and goes fast; closed Saturday and Sunday. There is no a la carte, so anyone who wants to order for themselves, or avoids seafood, should look elsewhere.
v-septime.person: Bertrand Grébaut (chef, ex-Arpège under Alain Passard; co-founded Septime in 2011 with high-school friend Théophile Pourriat)

signal_chip.label: No. 40, World's 50 Best 2025
signal_chip.full: Ranked No. 40 on The World's 50 Best Restaurants 2025 (also 1 MICHELIN star, Guide France 2026)

v-le-servan.name: Le Servan
v-le-servan.why: Two sisters born in Manila to a French father took over a gritty 1980s bar on rue Saint-Maur in 2014 and kept its zinc counter and hand-painted ceiling intact — French bones, a quiet Filipino accent laid over three-star technique.
v-le-servan.verdict: Go at lunch or for the late-afternoon zakouski and order the boudin-noir wontons under sweet chili and the chili-and-Thai-basil mussels; if the sauces and jus don't read as three-star discipline scaled down to bistro plates, the ex-Arpege / ex-Astrance pedigree is a line on a menu, not a kitchen.
v-le-servan.signature: Wontons de boudin noir, sauce chili doux (blood-sausage wontons, sweet chili) — the house zakouski, a standout singled out by The Infatuation and given its own dish page by Paris by Mouth.
v-le-servan.caveat: No new find: a twelve-year-old (opened spring 2014), hard-to-book institution whose marquee Le Fooding "Meilleur Bistrot" crown dates to 2015 — a decade old now. The room seats under 40, service runs Monday to Saturday only (no Sunday), and booking ahead is essential.

signal_chip.label: Le Fooding — Meilleur Bistrot 2015
signal_chip.full: Named Meilleur Bistrot 2015 by Le Fooding; still carried in the 2026 MICHELIN Guide and flagged by The Infatuation as one of its favorite little bistros in all of Paris.
signal_chip.cosign: Chef Tatiana Levha (b. 1984, Manila; French father, Filipino mother), trained under Alain Passard at L'Arpege and Pascal Barbot at L'Astrance, both three-Michelin-star; her sister Katia Levha runs the floor and the wine.

v-clown-bar.name: Clown Bar
v-clown-bar.why: The bar opened in 1902 two doors from the Cirque d'Hiver and was once the drinking hole of its acrobats and clowns; the 1920s Sarreguemines ceramic frieze that wraps the room is why circus performers, then chefs, kept coming back. History you can sit inside.
v-clown-bar.verdict: Order the cervelle de veau in chilled dashi — the one plate that never leaves the constantly-changing menu — and you eat Sota Atsumi's decade-old signature beneath a Sarreguemines ceramic clown frieze classé monument historique since 1995.
v-clown-bar.signature: Cervelle de veau: poached veal brain in a chilled dashi/ponzu broth finished with finely diced ginger and scallion. Added by Atsumi in 2014 and, by every account, the permanent fixture on an otherwise rotating card. The duck-and-foie-gras pithivier — breast, leg and foie gras in a caramelised crust — is the other order-it dish.
v-clown-bar.caveat: Two honest asterisks. The dining room is genuinely tiny and books out, so walk-ins rarely land a seat, and at bistro-plus prices with an offal-forward menu (brain, sweetbreads) this is a splurge, not a casual drop-in. And to correct the brief: Clown Bar is not on The Infatuation's current Best Bistros in Paris guide — its Infatuation review and Eater rave both date to 2016, so the press signal is real but aged.
v-clown-bar.person: Owners Sven Chartier & Ewen Lemoigne (also behind Saturne, 2e), who took over the historic bar in 2014 and installed Japanese chef Sota Atsumi — since departed to open his own Maison (2019). The kitchen has changed hands since; the current chef is reported as Korean-born Jung Yonghoon, though only via secondary listings, not an authority byline.

signal_chip.label: Infatuation + Eater · 2016
signal_chip.full: The Infatuation ran a standalone review (11 Dec 2016, by co-founder Chris Stang) calling it 'better than almost any other restaurant serving this kind of food in town'; Eater the same year named it 'the most thrilling restaurant in Paris.' Also carried on World's 50 Best Discovery (a directory listing, not a ranking). Note: absent from The Infatuation's current Best Bistros in Paris guide.

v-bistrot-paul-bert.name: Bistrot Paul Bert
v-bistrot-paul-bert.why: Bertrand Auboyneau was a finance man before he opened Paul Bert in 1997 with his wife Gwenaëlle Cadoret, building it into a standard-bearer for vigneron wine and unreconstructed bistro cooking under head chef Thierry Laurent.
v-bistrot-paul-bert.verdict: Still the dino-classic Paris bistrot Anthony Bourdain loved: the steak au poivre - coarse Sarawak pepper pressed into a thick cut of beef, finished in a cognac-cream sauce with crisp frites - is why you come, opened with complimentary gougeres and closed with a Paris-Brest. Falsifiable: it's phone-only and genuinely hard to land, closed Sunday and Monday, the room now runs heavily international, and at about 44 euros the steak divides critics on value - The Infatuation calls the branded merch and truffle-on-everything "a money grab."
v-bistrot-paul-bert.signature: Steak au poivre - a thick cut of beef crusted in coarsely cracked Sarawak pepper and finished in a cognac-cream sauce, with crisp frites; complimentary gougeres to open and a Paris-Brest to close.
v-bistrot-paul-bert.caveat: Reservations are by phone only and genuinely hard to land - the kitchen largely stopped answering the phone in fall 2022 as Bourdain-era demand overwhelmed it, and Paris by Mouth dropped it from its recommendations over the reservation chaos; the room now runs heavily international. In The Infatuation (Emily Monaco, 2024) the cooking still wins, but she flags the branded sweatshirts and truffle-on-everything as feeling like "a money grab"; on her own blog the same critic rates it good yet no better than similarly priced bistros such as Chez Georges. Steak au poivre runs about 44 euros. Closed Sunday and Monday.
v-bistrot-paul-bert.person: Bertrand Auboyneau - owner, a former finance man who opened Paul Bert in 1997 with his wife Gwenaelle Cadoret and built it into a standard-bearer for old-school bistro fare and vigneron-driven wine; kitchen led by head chef Thierry Laurent.

signal_chip.label: Bourdain: "one of the best"
signal_chip.full: On No Reservations, Anthony Bourdain: "there is no greater culinary institution in France than the old-school dino-style, unchanged-by-time classic Parisian bistro. And this place, Bistrot Paul Bert in the 11th, is one of the best." Also carried in the MICHELIN Guide at the Plate / "Good cooking" level (a Guide listing, not a star or Bib Gourmand) and listed by Gault&Millau (12/20).
signal_chip.cosign: Anthony Bourdain, No Reservations - documented by Time Out; full 2024 review by Emily Monaco in The Infatuation; authority listings in the MICHELIN Guide (Plate) & Gault&Millau

v-chez-l-ami-jean.name: Chez L'Ami Jean
v-chez-l-ami-jean.why: Stéphane Jégo spent a decade at Yves Camdeborde's La Régalade, one of bistronomie's founding kitchens, before taking over this Basque canteen in 2002 and running it like a rugby scrum — his baritone reaching you before the food does, and you come out full, a little deafened, and grinning.
v-chez-l-ami-jean.verdict: A fixture on The Infatuation's "The Best Bistros In Paris." Order the riz au lait: it arrives as one big bowl for the table, the salted-butter caramel and housemade nougatine in separate dishes for you to fold in yourself. In autumn and winter, wild game — roast grouse, wild boar stew — is the reason to book.
v-chez-l-ami-jean.signature: Riz au lait — vanilla rice pudding served tableside in a large bowl with salted-butter caramel sauce and housemade nougatine on the side to assemble your own
v-chez-l-ami-jean.caveat: Loud, cramped and expensive — The Infatuation's top ($$$$) tier: the sensory overload is the whole point, not a quiet or budget meal. Game is strictly seasonal (autumn–winter), so out of season you won't find it, and tables are tight — reserve well ahead.

signal_chip.label: The Infatuation · Best Bistros in Paris
signal_chip.full: Named to The Infatuation's 'The Best Bistros In Paris' guide (published June 9, 2026, by Emily Monaco), which singles out the wild game and the rice pudding; also carried — as a directory listing, not a ranking — on The World's 50 Best Discovery.

v-chez-georges.name: Chez Georges
v-chez-georges.why: Founded in 1964 by a patron named Georges, the room stayed in the same family for nearly fifty years until Jean-Gabriel de Bueil and Dominique Paul took it over in 2010 as its self-appointed guardians — changing, deliberately, nothing.
v-chez-georges.verdict: Old-Paris kept exactly where it was: on rue du Mail since 1964, the menu still handwritten in looping French script, the salade lyonnaise still arriving as a shared bowl heavy with thumb-sized lardons, the foie de veau still landing beside a mound of shoestring frites. Lunch and dinner on weekdays only - dark every Saturday and Sunday, and closed for the August holidays. Weekday, or not at all.
v-chez-georges.signature: Foie de veau - a thick slab of calf's liver - served beside a mound of shoestring frites, after the escargots and a shared bowl of salade lyonnaise heavy with thumb-sized lardons.
v-chez-georges.caveat: Not cheap and not cuddly. The Infatuation rates it $$$$ and calls the wine list "ultimately overpriced," with service that blends "efficiency, practiced scorn, and flirtiness." There is no online booking - you call, re-call, email, or turn up in person - and beware the several unrelated Paris restaurants that share the name (one of them a vegetarian spot); only rue du Mail is this one.
v-chez-georges.person: Jean-Gabriel de Bueil - the hands-on owner-guardian (The Infatuation names him the bistro's "committed guardian"); he and Dominique Paul bought Chez Georges in 2010. It was founded in 1964 by its namesake Georges and stayed in the same family until they took over.

signal_chip.full: The Infatuation (Mar 18, 2026): a $$$$ "time warp" bistro whose handwritten menu is written "in a looping French penmanship that hasn't been taught since the '60s"; Jean-Gabriel de Bueil named its "committed guardian."
